article.headline: The Second-Tier Memory Bet That the AI Supercycle May Vindicate
article.lede: The biggest names in DRAM are busy making chips for artificial intelligence — leaving the commodity market thin and the smaller Taiwanese, Chinese, and Japanese producers looking like unlikely beneficiaries of a squeeze they did not engineer.
article.body:
Memory semiconductors have always been a cyclical business, but cycles have moods. The current one has a particular quality: it is being driven not by a consumer electronics boom or a server-refresh wave but by the voracious appetite of AI accelerators for a specific, exotic variety of DRAM called **High Bandwidth Memory** (HBM) — a 3D-stacked chip that sits directly alongside a GPU die and moves data at speeds standard memory cannot approach. The trouble, for everyone else in the market, is that HBM is extraordinarily wasteful of manufacturing capacity. A single gigabyte of HBM3 consumes roughly three times the silicon wafer area of an equivalent gigabyte of standard DDR5, and current production yields hover between 50 and 60 percent. Every rack of Nvidia H100s or B200s is thus quietly cannibalizing the factory floor that would otherwise produce PC RAM, server DIMMs, or the commodity flash chips used in smartphones.

The arithmetic compounds quickly. By TrendForce's estimate, HBM and GDDR7 (a high-speed graphics memory variant) will account for nearly 20 percent of all global DRAM wafer capacity in 2026, up from a sliver three years ago. SK Hynix, which controls roughly 60 percent of the HBM market, and Samsung have each reallocated up to 40 percent of their advanced-node capacity toward these AI products. The consequence — familiar to anyone who has tried to price a server build recently — is a commodity DRAM market where buyers receive less than half of their requested wafer allocations and inventory has shrunk to approximately eight weeks of supply. Contract DRAM prices rose more than 33 percent in average selling price terms year-on-year, with some legacy grades up over 200 percent since early 2025.

It is into this gap that the smaller players step. The tweet's logic is straightforward: Nanya Technology (2408.TW), Winbond (2344.TW), and Macronix (2337.TW) in Taiwan; SanDisk (SNDK) in NAND flash; Kioxia (285A.T) in Japan; and the Chinese state-backed duo of **YMTC** (Yangtze Memory Technologies, in NAND) and **CXMT** (ChangXin Memory Technologies, in DRAM) — none of them are meaningfully present in HBM. What they *do* make is the commodity memory that the Korean giants are quietly vacating. Nanya's April 2026 revenue came in at NT$25.5 billion, up 717 percent year-on-year, a figure that reads like a misprint but was confirmed as a record by the company itself. Winbond, after four consecutive quarters of losses, returned to full utilization and profitability in Q3 2025 and expects a healthy outlook through 2026. Even Macronix, a NOR flash specialist (NOR flash is a smaller, faster type used in automotive and industrial devices rather than bulk data storage), is sampling three-dimensional NOR products ahead of a 2027 production ramp.

Kioxia listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in December 2024 at ¥1,455 per share and promptly swung from a ¥244 billion net loss to a ¥272 billion net profit in fiscal year 2024, its best result since separating from Toshiba in 2018. SanDisk — spun out from Western Digital in February 2025 — has been the most dramatic case: shares rose more than 2,400 percent in roughly fifteen months, as the market re-rated a hardware manufacturer into a pure-play semiconductor story at the precise moment NAND prices were recovering. The rally has drawn skepticism from Wells Fargo, which sees the stock as priced for perfection, and a 247 Wall St. analysis in April 2026 put fair value roughly 32 percent below current levels — a reminder that asymmetric upside does not mean unlimited upside.

The Chinese producers are the most politically freighted part of the thesis. CXMT's monthly DRAM output grew from 100,000 wafers at the start of 2024 to 290,000 by year-end 2025, and the company reported 2025 revenue of roughly $8 billion — a 130 percent surge. YMTC, primarily a NAND maker, is on track to become the world's third-largest NAND producer by output by late 2026, and has reportedly begun exploring HBM using *through-silicon via* (TSV) technology, the stacking technique that defines the product. Both companies remain private and face U.S. export restrictions on advanced chipmaking equipment, which puts a ceiling on how quickly they can close the process-node gap with their Korean and Japanese rivals. Their expansion, however, adds a geopolitical wrinkle to the supercycle: if Chinese capacity floods the commodity DRAM and NAND markets at the same moment Korean supply normalizes, the squeeze that is today lifting all boats could reverse sharply.

The honest caveat is that memory supercycles have a habit of ending badly for latecomers. Capacity that looks scarce in 2025 gets built, and DRAM has a particular talent for overshooting — the industry spent most of 2022 and 2023 drowning in surplus. The structural case for this cycle being more durable than its predecessors rests on HBM's continued absorption of wafer capacity through multiple product generations (HBM4, expected in volume by late 2026, and HBM4E after that), and on the inference-driven growth in data-center NAND as AI models are deployed at scale rather than merely trained. Whether that structural argument survives contact with CXMT's expansion timeline, or with the next macroeconomic downturn, is precisely the kind of uncertainty that the tweet does not resolve — but at least frames correctly.

concepts.definition: A three-dimensional DRAM architecture in which multiple memory dies are stacked vertically and connected by microscopic through-silicon vias, then placed directly alongside a GPU or AI accelerator in the same chip package. HBM delivers data to processors far faster than conventional DRAM but consumes two to three times the wafer manufacturing capacity per gigabyte, creating a supply drain on the broader DRAM market whenever AI chip production scales up.

A sustained, multi-year period of above-normal pricing and demand for semiconductor memory, typically driven by a structural shift in end-market consumption rather than a seasonal or inventory-led bump. The current cycle is attributed to AI-accelerator demand for HBM diverting wafer capacity away from commodity DRAM and NAND, tightening supply for all categories simultaneously.

A type of non-volatile (data-retaining without power) flash memory optimized for fast random reads and in-place code execution, used primarily in automotive control units, industrial sensors, and networking equipment. It is smaller in capacity but more reliable and faster-access than NAND flash, which dominates bulk storage applications like SSDs and smartphones.

A vertical electrical connection that passes through an entire silicon die, enabling memory chips to be stacked and wired together in three dimensions. TSV technology is the core manufacturing technique behind HBM and is difficult to execute at scale; it requires specialized equipment and expertise that Chinese chipmakers are attempting to develop domestically.

The current mainstream generation of double-data-rate DRAM used in personal computers and servers. It succeeds DDR4, offering higher bandwidth and lower power consumption, and is increasingly the baseline memory type for AI servers that do not require the extreme bandwidth of HBM.

article.fact_check: The core figures — HBM consuming ~20% of DRAM wafer capacity in 2026, Nanya April 2026 revenue up 717% YoY, CXMT at 290,000 wafers/month by end-2025, SanDisk up 2,400%+ since February 2025 spinoff, Kioxia FY2024 net profit of ¥272.3 billion — are sourced from TrendForce, Digitimes, and company announcements and are consistent across multiple industry outlets. The figure that HBM consumes ~3x wafer capacity per GB versus standard DRAM is widely cited by Tom's Hardware, NextPlatform, and analyst notes and is considered reliable. The claim that YMTC will become the world's third-largest NAND producer by late 2026 by output is an analyst projection (multiple sources including TechInsights and TechWire Asia) and carries forward-looking uncertainty. The Chinese producers' revenue figures are drawn from public reports but cannot be independently audited given their private status.

ticker_2337-tw.name: Macronix International Co., Ltd.
ticker_2337-tw.blurb: Macronix International Co., Ltd. is a Taiwanese semiconductor company specializing in non-volatile memory solutions, including NOR Flash, NAND Flash, and ROM products. The company is a leading global supplier of NOR Flash memory, serving applications in consumer electronics, automotive, industrial, and networking. Macronix focuses on advanced memory technologies such as 3D NAND and high-density NOR Flash to maintain its competitive position.
ticker_2337-tw.recent: In the past 30 days, Macronix's stock has experienced volatility amid broader semiconductor market trends. The company reported its monthly sales for February 2025, showing a decline compared to the previous year, reflecting weak demand in consumer electronics. Analysts have noted ongoing challenges in the memory market but highlight Macronix's potential in automotive and industrial segments.

ticker_sndk.name: SanDisk Corporation
ticker_sndk.blurb: SanDisk was spun off from Western Digital in February 2025 as an independent pure-play NAND flash memory company. It designs and manufactures NAND-based solid-state drives, flash storage chips, and consumer memory products. The spinoff allowed the market to re-rate the business on semiconductor multiples rather than hardware-manufacturer multiples, contributing to an extraordinary post-spinoff rally driven by the NAND supercycle.
ticker_sndk.recent: Since its February 2025 spinoff, SNDK surged over 2,400% through May 2026, reaching an all-time high above $1,189. Fiscal year 2025 revenue was approximately $7.4 billion, with gross margins expanding to ~36% from the low 20s in late 2024, aided by a shift toward high-margin QLC (quad-level cell) products. Analyst targets range from $975 (Wells Fargo, Equal Weight) to $1,250 (Bernstein SocGen, Outperform). A 247 Wall St. analysis in April 2026 flagged potential overvaluation of ~32% versus peers.

ticker_285a-t.name: Kioxia Holdings Corporation
ticker_285a-t.blurb: Kioxia Holdings Corporation is a Japanese memory solutions provider, known for its NAND flash memory and solid-state drives (SSDs). The company was spun off from Toshiba in 2018 and is one of the world's largest NAND flash memory manufacturers. It competes with industry leaders like Samsung and Western Digital in the semiconductor memory market.
ticker_285a-t.recent: In the past 30 days, Kioxia's stock price has shown volatility amid broader semiconductor market trends. The company has benefited from increased NAND demand visibility and disciplined capital spending, as noted by Morningstar. No major earnings or news events were reported in the last month.
